claims.text: The target quaternary equiatomic alloy is a single-phase FCC solid solution.
Vacuum arc melting followed by annealing will produce a homogeneous target alloy.
Between 673 K and 873 K, the target alloy's yield strength will become insensitive to strain rate.
The intermediate-temperature yield-strength plateau is caused by dominance of edge-dislocation glide.
Edge dislocations can control the strength of refractory BCC high-entropy alloys.
The refractory NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy provides the basis for assigning the target plateau to 673–873 K.
At cryogenic temperatures, deformation will occur through a combination of dislocation glide and deformation twinning.
Cryogenic deformation twinning and high-stress glide will significantly increase strain-rate sensitivity.
Cross-slip has a high activation energy in the target alloy at 673–873 K.
At 673–873 K, thermal activation overcomes glide barriers sufficiently that yield strength becomes independent of strain rate.
At low temperatures, insufficient thermal activation forces deformation toward athermal twinning or high-stress dislocation glide.
Below 673 K, yield strength will increase significantly as strain rate increases.
Above 873 K, yield strength will decrease with temperature and may recover strain-rate sensitivity because of diffusion-controlled creep.
Standard dislocation-glide theory predicts that yield strength decreases with temperature and increases with strain rate.
C or Mo microalloying can induce FCC-to-HCP or FCC-to-BCC transformation during deformation in Co-Cr-Fe-Ni alloys.
In dual-phase FCC/B2 alloys, phase boundaries dominate deformation.
Differences in stacking-fault energy and lattice friction between BCC refractory alloys and the target FCC alloy may shift the plateau temperature.
A strain-rate sensitivity exponent greater than 0.01 at 773 K would falsify the predicted strain-rate-insensitive plateau.
Observation of an FCC-to-HCP or FCC-to-BCC transformation at 773 K would falsify the proposed purely dislocation-glide mechanism.

contradictions.description: The primary intervention specifies uniaxial tensile testing, whereas the proposed in-situ TEM alternative uses compression; compression may activate a different deformation response and is not a simultaneous observation of the stated tensile test.
